https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/08/12/t.text: TMT Newswire GlobeNewswire INVL Fund and Tesonet to Jointly Acquire Šiaurės Licėjus Schools and Kindergartens By GlobeNewswire August 12, 2026 20 Resize Small Medium Large Technology Group Tesonet and one of the leading private equity funds in Central and Eastern Europe, INVL Private Equity Fund II, having decided earlier this year to invest jointly in the private education sector, will acquire the Šiaurės Licėjus network of schools and kindergartens. The companies will execute the project through a joint venture Kurianti Karta. This transaction aims to develop high-quality private education in Lithuania that meets contemporary needs. The transaction is expected to close by the end of 2026, subject to approval from the Lithuanian Competition Council. Šiaurės Licėjus, which launched operations more than a decade ago, currently operates two schools, three kindergartens, and a swimming pool and extracurricular activities center in Vilnius. Nearly one thousand students and kindergarteners attend the school and kindergarten facilities. The incoming owners are committed to building a high-quality learning ecosystem. "To achieve the highest standard of education, it is essential to create the best conditions for it to flourish. This matters to us personally - this is our home - so we see this not merely as a business investment, but as a drive to directly contribute to an environment and the opportunities that will nurture a free-thinking, creative, and courageous generation, and to help improve and expand both quality and accessibility," says Eglė Eidimtaitė, Head of Investments at the Tesonet Group. "The examples of many of the world's most successful countries demonstrate that private investment enhances the quality of education and creates value for society and investors alike. Together with the Tesonet team, we aim to create the conditions for the school and kindergarten network to grow by investing in infrastructure and continuously raising the standard of education," says Nerijus Drobavičius, Partner at INVL Private Equity Fund II. Eglė Sidorova, Head of Šiaurės Licėjus, notes that the arrival of a new strategic partner represents a meaningful recognition of the organization's journey to date - and, at the same time, an opportunity to plan the future with even greater ambition. In recent years, Šiaurės Licėjus has consistently invested in growth. The school and kindergarten in Didžioji Riešė are already operating in a new, modern building featuring dedicated learning, sports, and swimming pool facilities, and within the next year the Central campus plans to relocate to entirely new school, kindergarten, and swimming pool premises. Advertisement "This decision is an important recognition for us, one that confirms that the educational system built over many years of dedicated work, the team we have assembled, and the trust of our community carry clear long-term value. We are gaining a strong partner with whom we can invest consistently in educational quality, the learning environment, and our educators' professional growth. What matters most to us is that students, parents, and staff experience this change as an opportunity to grow, while preserving the values and educational direction of Šiaurės Licėjus," says E. Sidorova. Šiaurės Licėjus generated EUR 8.8 million in revenue in the 2025-2026 academic year, and the group employs approximately 180 people. The buyer's financial advisor was Forvis Mazars, and its legal advisor was Motieka & Audzevičius. The seller's legal advisors were Glimstedt. About INVL Private Equity Fund II With EUR 410 million of commitments, this is one of the leading private equity funds in Central and Eastern Europe. The fund is sector-agnostic and is looking to build a diversified portfolio investing in companies with the potential to become regional leaders in their respective industries. Equity tickets range between EUR 10 million and EUR 60 million, though larger tickets are possible with co-investors. The fund is seeking majority or significant minority stakes where it could drive long-term value creation. The focus is on businesses with strong potential to grow and compete amid intensifying global competition. Geographically, the fund is targeting opportunities in the Baltic countries, Poland, and the broader European Union. Advertisement The fund is managed by INVL Asset Management, the leading Baltic alternative asset manager, which is a part of the Invalda INVL Group with over 30 years of experience. The group’s companies manage or have under supervision EUR 2.1 billion in assets across a diverse range of investment strategies, including private equity, forests and agricultural land, renewable energy, real estate, and private debt. Additionally, the group provides family office services in Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, manages pension funds in Latvia, and invests in global third-party funds. About Tesonet Tesonet is a business developer and investor that has helped grow two Lithuanian unicorns: cybersecurity market leaders NordSecurity + Surfshark, and the internet data infrastructure group Oxylabs. Over a year ago, Tesonet launched the artificial intelligence platform nexos.ai, and companies nurtured within its ecosystem now employ more than 4,200 professionals. Since 2018, Tesonet has also been actively investing in a broader portfolio of companies, including Hostinger, Artea, BC Žalgiris, BC Lions Club, Cast AI, Eneba, Turing College, Lovable, and others. Advertisement About Šiaurės licėjus Šiaurės Licėjus is a private network of schools and kindergartens in Vilnius, educating children from one year of age through 12th grade. The network comprises schools in Vilnius city centre and Didžioji Riešė, three kindergartens, and a complex featuring a swimming pool and an extracurricular activities centre. The educational philosophy of Šiaurės Licėjus is rooted in Nordic education principles, balancing child well-being with academic achievement through integrated and experiential learning as well as social and emotional development. The school was the first in Lithuania to implement phenomenon-based learning. Its Nordic approach to education is captured in the school's motto: "Happy children learn better." Today, the Šiaurės Licėjus community numbers nearly one thousand students and kindergarteners, supported by 180 staff members. Since the previous academic year, the Didžioji Riešė school has been operating in a modern, architecturally distinctive building where learning spaces are seamlessly integrated with sports, swimming pool, and leisure areas. By September 2027, the city centre school will also open its doors in a state-of-the-art building designed to meet not only today's educational needs but those of the future as well. https://balkaninsight.com/2026/09/02/thi.text: Hungarians share stories about family breakdowns, painful personal experiences, career endings and loss of loved ones, in an oral history archive chronicling life under Fidesz. When Luca Varadi watched the news about the landslide defeat of the Fidesz party at Hungary’s April 12 general election, her first reaction was one of euphoria: 16 years of Viktor Orban’s rule were finally over. But her joy was soon tempered by feelings of anger and frustration. “What’s the price we had to pay for all those years? What has it all taken away from us?” she asked herself. Varadi, a sociologist and associate professor at the Vienna-based Central European University (CEU), poured her feelings out in a Facebook post that went viral in Hungary. People shared similar mixed feelings and more: stories about families torn apart, painful personal experiences, abrupt career endings, and the loss of loved ones. “There has been so much written about democratic backsliding and the erosion of democratic institutions, but so little about how this system really impacted on people’s personal lives,” Varadi tells BIRN in an interview. Rather spontaneously, she decided to launch the Igy eltunk itt (“This Is How We Lived Here”) initiative with her fellow researcher, Tamas Kohut. Essentially an oral history archive, the two are currently conducting personal interviews with people who have registered to share their stories. It’s a meticulous exercise. So far, they have received more than 240 submissions and conducted 54 interviews, but their target is at least 400 to have a diverse sample of different age groups and professions, spanning the country. The interviews will be edited and published online – possibly also in book format – as a memento of one of the most consequential periods of Hungarian modern history. “I believe this is not only about Hungary,” she says. “These stories are vivid examples of what democratic backsliding and the emptying of democratic institutions can really do to people’s everyday lives. Not just in Hungary, but anywhere.” When Varadi discusses the interviews, she becomes emotional. People share with her their losses, their pain, their sacrifices and often their moral dilemmas. “The losses are not abstract; they are palpable,” she says. Facebook page of Így éltünk itt – közösségi archívum. Magyarország, 2010-2026 Forced into exile Edit and Peter were among the first to register for Varadi’s project to share their experiences. This couple with a small child once had a comfortable life in a mid-sized provincial town in Hungary. Edit was a popular German teacher at a local school, where her students cherished her. But she was also an outspoken critic when it came to politics, and she stood up for academic freedom when the Fidesz government started to roll back teachers’ autonomy and implement education reforms. Edit became increasingly uncomfortable for her colleagues. An atmosphere of silence and tension surrounded her at school, while parents criticised her because of her political views. Ultimately, she gave up and quit her job – and the country. She moved to Germany where she now teaches German to refugees. Soon after, her husband, once a journalist in the local media, joined her. Now he delivers frozen vegetables to earn a living, leaving behind his journalistic ambitions. Edit lost her mother while living abroad, a loss they can hardly forgive themselves for. “This is a painful experience that comes up very often. Practically with all the people who felt forced to leave Hungary, the trauma is there: leaving behind loved ones,” Varadi explains. Close to 400,000 people left Hungary over the last 16 years. While most moved for higher wages and better career opportunities, Varadi’s interviews also show that many departed to escape the political system. Emigration was one of the most common survival strategies. The new Tisza government is trying to lure them back, but many may opt to “wait and see”. There have been some early returners, though. “We talked to a former university lecturer who gave up her career and left because she could not face the hate-mongering political billboards all around the country,” Varadi recounts. This academic sold everything and left for Belgium, a country whose language she did not even speak, to care for the elderly. The election night of April 12 changed her life again. “This is my home, I am coming back,” she told Varadi. She was going to pack her belongings and return Hungary to start afresh, with no job or house to return to. Studios of Hungary’s Media Services and Support Trust Fund: Photo: MTVA Those who stayed The vast majority, of course, stayed in Hungary and adopted different survival strategies. A journalist working for Hungary’s public service broadcaster confessed to Varadi that now he feels he was a coward. He was “only” responsible for cultural content, did not have to do political reporting, but he was one of the hundreds who helped operate what many now refer to as “a factory of lies and propaganda” on state channels. “I never crossed a professional red line myself,” he justifies in the interview, but goes on to admit that he earned a good salary that afforded him and his family a comfortable life. While many talk about intimidation, self-censorship and adaption to the system, some stories prove that courage did sometimes pay off. A man who worked on development projects in a provincial town described the mounting pressure he felt from local authorities to award projects – and the public money that came with them – to Fidesz-aligned companies. Yet he did not bow, and decided to maintain strict application criteria. He was prepared to be fired, but to his surprise nothing happened. There were no reprisals. The conversations often take a turn and raise questions about individual or joint responsibility. “Many people ask the question how could this all happen to us? And above all: why did we let it happen?” Varadi says. Did Hungarian society simply follow the century-old patterns of making compromises, adapting and succumbing to pressure in order to survive, as was done under the rule of the Turks, the Habsburgs and the Soviets? “One thing is for sure: there were no guns pointed at people’s heads,” Peter Kreko, director of the Budapest-based Political Capital, tells BIRN. Kreko, a social psychologist, finds it perhaps most surprising that Orban managed to keep his grip on power for 16 years without resorting to violence, primarily through the manipulation of information. “This was a perfect ‘information autocracy’,” he says. Kreko believes people always had a choice, and this was especially true for those working for the state media or the public administration. But many followed what historian Timothy Snyder has described as ‘anticipatory obedience’: trying to figure out what is expected of them and behave accordingly. When it comes to conformism or adaptation, Kreko says, Hungary is not very different from its regional peers, but it is certainly true that Hungarian society has a historical tendency to bow to authoritarian leaders. “What we see is that many people were afraid, felt intimidated,” is how Varadi explains it. Many feared negative consequences if they spoke up. Many sacrificed their right to free speech for their comfortable lives. And by doing so, many became accomplices of the system. Stefano Bottoni, an Italian-Hungarian historian researching Central European modern history, points to the general lack of solidarity and mistrust in Hungarian society. “There were no institutions people would have trusted. The most common channel to rebel against the system was to write angry Facebook posts,” Bottoni tells BIRN. He believes stronger trade unions, something like Solidarity in Poland in the 1980s, would have helped build critical communities, but they are virtually non-existent in Hungary. “We helped weaken the resilience of the system, believing that we don’t need those institutions, we will figure out a survival method all by ourselves,” he says. Varadi shares this analysis: “Many people felt powerless and left alone. When the teachers went on to strike there was virtually no solidarity from the society.” Hungarian PM and leader of the ruling Fidesz party Viktor Orban (L), speaking during an anti-war rally organized by the Digital Civic Circles in Miskolc, Hungary, 17 January 2026. EPA/AKOS KAISER/HANDOUT Lessons for the future Varadi and Kohut’s This is How We Lived Here is not just a project about the past. They hope it can help the next generation – in Hungary but also elsewhere – understand what happened and avoid committing the same mistakes. The social psychologist Kreko also believes it is very important for Hungarian society to confront the past 16 years and also to take responsibility for having allowed this system to emerge and take root. The historian Bottoni argues that confronting the past and carrying out the lustration Hungary lacked after 1990 are absolutely vital, but so too is building a culture of critical debate, perhaps even within families. Varadi and Kohut have listened to dozens of stories about families and friendships breaking apart as political hate-mongering poisoned people’s everyday lives. “A woman who joined an NGO was attacked by her grandmother as a traitor betraying her country. She had to walk on eggshells to avoid anything politics or work related,” Varadi says. This woman was lucky compared to others who suffered total estrangement with family because of differing political views. Varadi hopes their project can help heal some of the wounds inflicted during the last 16 years and, above all, document the individual price we all pay when living under authoritarian regimes. “So much energy wasted on compromises and individual survival strategies – such a huge loss,” she sighs. U.S. District Judge Jennifer L. Rochon in New York sided with a coalition, including the nonpartisan watchdog Common Cause, that challenged the ads as an illegal misuse of funds. She told the administration to cancel any remaining ads, including any set to air Sunday night, in granting a temporary restraining order. “Defendants shall not enter into, renew, or expand any agreement authorizing the development, creation, dissemination, placement, or airing of the challenged advertisements” during the two-week duration of her order, the judge said. Asked for comment, the White House referred to an Oct. 5 social media post from Trump in which he defended the taxpayer-funded ads as “rather standard” but, amid backlash, said he would pay for them from his political fundraising. In a court filing late Saturday, the Justice Department argued that the temporary restraining order was unnecessary because “the alleged offending conduct will end tomorrow.” The Department of Homeland Security tapped $20 million in taxpayer money for the ads. Legal experts have suggested that violated a federal statute against congressionally appropriated money being used for “publicity or propaganda” and potentially other laws. Isaias moves north into Appalachians and mid-Atlantic; Southern California battered by Rachel PENSACOLA, Fla. (AP) — People in the Florida Panhandle and southern Alabama cleaned up after Hurricane Isaias swept through as the storm's remnants caused flooding in North Carolina on Sunday, while powerful Pacific Ocean waves stirred up by Rachel, a former tropical storm, battered the coast of Southern California. In western North Carolina, rivers overflowed as heavy rainfall raised the risk of flash and urban flooding, according to the National Weather Service. It said tornadoes were possible in parts of Virginia and North Carolina as well as dangerous surf and rip current conditions along the Gulf and southeastern Atlantic coasts. At least four deaths were linked to Isaias, the first hurricane of the Atlantic season, which came ashore as a Category 2 hurricane Friday near Destin, Florida, a Gulf Coast vacation spot filled with high-rises and tourist shops. The storm then roared into Alabama with tropical-force winds before heading farther north. In Florida’s Escambia County, Sheriff Chip Simmons said a woman was killed when a tree fell on her home and a man died of carbon monoxide fumes from a generator running in his garage. One person died when a tree fell on a house in Birmingham, said Cory Moon, the city’s fire chief. A second storm-related death in Alabama was attributed to a motor vehicle crash involving a downed tree in Barbour County, said Josh Johnson of the state’s emergency management agency. Hurricane Simon pounds resorts and vulnerable towns along Mexico’s Pacific coast PUERTO VALLARTA, Mexico (AP) — Hurricane Simon pounded Mexico’s Pacific coast as a Category 3 storm on Sunday, its eye remaining just offshore as its most powerful winds and rain slammed people living between the Sierra Madre and the ocean. The hurricane's center swirled parallel to the coast, closing in on the Puerto Vallarta area, where its most damaging winds and rain were expected to hit around midnight and continue through Monday morning. Its maximum sustained winds weakened Sunday to 125 mph (205 kph), according to the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami, but it was still expected to remain a dangerous hurricane. That’s not good news for people in and around Puerto Vallarta, a popular tourist destination in the state of Jalisco. Just inland and uphill from the resort areas, many Mexicans live in communities where housing might not stand up to the storm. By Sunday afternoon, Simon's eye was moving northwest about 50 miles (80 kilometers) south of Cabo Corrientes at about 5 mph (7 kph). A senior hurricane center specialist, Phillipe Pappin, said this westernmost tip of mainland Mexico is the area most likely to get a direct hit from the system. Cabo Corrientes is at the southern tip of Bahia de Banderas, the wide bay where Puerto Vallarta looks out to the Pacific. Hurricane-force winds extend outward up to 25 miles (35 kilometers), and tropical-storm-force winds reach up to 60 miles (95 kilometers) from Simon’s center, meaning the entire area between Mexico's western coast and the Sierra Madre mountains could be affected. Pope Leo XIV will have surgery in the coming days to remove a nodule on his lung VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV announced Sunday he will undergo surgery “in the coming days” to remove a nodule on his lung, in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. The 71-year-old Leo said the nodule was found at an early stage and was “circumscribed” or small and well-localized. The Vatican said Leo's expected recovery time from surgery would be a week. The American pope made the announcement during his Sunday noon blessing in an unusual display of transparency about his health. He thanked the crowd for their closeness and entrusted himself to their prayers. The Vatican didn’t say exactly when the surgery would take place, other than in the early days of this week. Leo has one upcoming main event: the closing Mass on Wednesday of a weeklong conference on family ministry, but Vatican officials suggested he might miss it. A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 3 centimeters (1 inch) that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen, according to the American Cancer Society. Often, the scans are done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening. Saudi airport passenger terminal is struck again, a day after 12 were killed CAIRO (AP) — A projectile struck a passenger terminal at the international airport in Riyadh on Sunday, a day after a missile hit the same terminal and killed 12 people, the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen said. The Houthis claimed responsibility for those attacks and others. Saudi authorities said there were injuries in the latest attack on the King Khalid International Airport complex for terminals 3 and 4, serving domestic flights. The airport — struck four times in the past five days — has been closed since Saturday’s missile attack, which was the deadliest in a Gulf Arab nation since the Iran war began. Over 300 other people were wounded, some critically. The sharp escalation in the war's new front threatens to draw in greater U.S. military involvement. President Donald Trump has said he is weighing joining the fight against the Houthis. There was no White House comment Sunday. India’s embassy in Saudi Arabia said one of its citizens died Sunday of injuries sustained in Saturday’s attack, which would bring the toll to 13. Saudi authorities later said King Fahd International Airport in Dammam also was attacked, with few details. The city is on the Persian Gulf near Bahrain and Qatar. The latest strike in Riyadh came shortly after the Houthis said the airport in the rebel-held Yemeni capital of Sanaa had been struck again, and blamed the Saudis. On Sunday night the Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV channel reported further strikes on Sanaa, blaming Saudi Arabia. Saudi Arabia has not commented on the strikes. AP source: Trump, Rubio weigh firing US envoy to Greece after mounting reports of improper conduct WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are considering firing U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle after a series of reports alleging she has engaged in improper and possibly illegal conduct before and during her tenure in Athens. A senior U.S. official said Sunday that Trump and Rubio are “extremely pissed off” by Guilfoyle’s reported conduct and would likely decide on what action to take this week after Monday’s Columbus Day holiday. The official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal deliberations, said Rubio had been particularly angry, not least because he visited Athens just last week and Guilfoyle attended most, if not all, of his events and greeted him on his arrival with a bear hug as the allegations swirled. In a series of stories, The Wall Street Journal has reported questionable conduct by Guilfoyle, including an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to use her influence inside the administration in return for the payment of a large credit card bill. Guilfoyle has not addressed the reports directly, although her lawyer has said she did nothing wrong and the U.S. Embassy in Athens has tacitly expressed support for her. Pennsylvania shooter who killed 8 was family’s patriarch, father of toddler killed says ERIE, Pa. (AP) — A man whose toddler was among eight people killed in a mass shooting in Erie, Pennsylvania, said Sunday that the gunman was a grandfather who never seemed distressed or out of the ordinary. “I think that was a front for him,” Julius Windham said as he stood at a memorial to victims of Friday’s shooting, including his 1-year-old daughter Amarianna, her pregnant mother and the woman’s 5-year-old son and unborn baby. “Him every day, him smiling and being just — you would think of nothing like that would happen,” Windham said. The 45-year-old gunman took his own life. Authorities have not released his name, but Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah said he was related to seven of the victims. The eighth was a friend of the pregnant woman, he said. Police have not made their names public, either. Mourners on Sunday placed candles, flowers and stuffed animals outside the home where the man opened fire shortly before 5 p.m. Friday. Windham wore a T-shirt with pictures of the women and children and the words, “Forever In My Heart.” Trump says Russia and Ukraine agree to an ‘energy ceasefire’ but Kyiv says attacks continue WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. President Donald Trump said Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an “energy ceasefire” in the 4 1/2-year-old war, but he offered no details on it and Kyiv reported attacks by Moscow on energy sites after his statement. Trump’s brief social media post said only that the ceasefire took effect immediately, adding: “Do not break it!” Moscow did not immediately comment. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that while his country “welcomed” the announcement by Trump as “good news for everyone,” Russia was still hitting energy infrastructure in Kyiv and in the city of Kharkiv. “Unfortunately, Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian ‘shaheds’ all day today,” he said in an evening address, referring to drones launched by Moscow . “There have been glide bomb strikes and strikes on our energy infrastructure too. A power plant in Kharkiv was attacked this evening.” The presidential office confirmed the Kharkiv attack came after Trump's ceasefire post. Six senators call for Trump administration to 'immediately reverse course' on Russian diesel plan WASHINGTON (AP) — A bipartisan group of six senators on Sunday called for President Donald Trump's administration to “immediately reverse course” on a plan to purchase diesel from Russia as part of an effort to lower high fuel prices. Trump shocked lawmakers when he announced on social media Friday that he struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call. He said Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to the American and global market, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote. Four Republican senators and two Democratic senators signed onto the statement released Sunday in protesting the deal. They said the administration failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute. “The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course,” they wrote. The Republican senators who signed onto the statement are Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah. The Democratic senators are Sens. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut. Georgia takes over at No. 1 in AP Top 25 with Notre Dame, Miami next; Oregon is out of the poll Georgia moved up to No. 1 in The Associated Press Top 25 on Sunday following its win at Alabama, Texas dropped six spots to No. 7 after its loss to rival Oklahoma and Oregon was unranked for the first time in four years after losing for the second time in the past month. The Bulldogs, who had been No. 2 for five straight polls while rolling off five straight lopsided wins, went on the road and beat Alabama 20-17 with the help of what appeared to be a missed pass interference call in the end zone late in the game. Georgia received 66 first-place votes from the panel of 70 media members after its first victory in Tuscaloosa since 2014 and ascended to the top of the poll for the first time since Sept. 8, 2024. Notre Dame, which tuned up for this week's top-10 matchup at BYU with a 58-7 rout of Stanford, moved up one spot to No. 2. The Fighting Irish got one first-place vote and have their highest ranking since they were No. 2 in the final poll of the 2024 season. No. 3 Miami, which received two first-place votes, is followed by Ohio State and Indiana. The Hoosiers, who received the remaining first-place vote, got a two-spot promotion after their narrow win at Nebraska. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.
